summary: This informational note describes the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme, a hash-based digital signature system based on existing scientific literature. It specifies WOTS+, a one-time signature scheme, XMSS as a single-tree scheme, and the multi-tree variant XMSS^MT. Such schemes are of interest because they rely on hash functions.

eli5.summary: A signature that is built only from scrambling machines, not tricky math. It uses many one-use stamps arranged in a tree so you can sign many things.

subtitle: A digital signature built only from hash functions, using a tree of one-time keys to sign many messages.

tldr.problem: Common signature schemes such as RSA, DSA and ECDSA rely on hard mathematical problems. Hash-based signatures rely only on a hash function and are of interest for their resistance to quantum-computer-aided attacks.
tldr.mechanism: WOTS+ signs one message per key. XMSS places 2^h WOTS+ key pairs at the leaves of a Merkle tree whose root is the public key, and XMSS^MT stacks several such trees to speed up key generation.
tldr.outcome: The schemes are stateful: the private key changes with every signature, and reusing a key state destroys all security guarantees. The RFC is Informational and from the IRTF.

today: RFC 8391 is an Informational RFC from the IRTF's Crypto Forum Research Group, published in May 2018, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The text itself says deployments need systems that prevent reuse of secret key states.

sections.title: Hash-Based Signatures and XMSS
sections.content:
A digital signature scheme lets someone sign a message with a private key so others can verify it with a public key. A One-Time Signature (OTS) scheme can sign exactly one message securely per key pair. A Many-Time Signature (MTS) system signs several. Such schemes, proposed by Merkle in 1979, are called hash-based signature schemes because they are built from a cryptographic hash function.

The RFC lists their traits: small private and public keys, and fast signing and verification, but large signatures and relatively slow key generation. They are also described as naturally resistant to most side-channel attacks.

RFC 8391 describes WOTS+ (a one-time scheme), single-tree XMSS and the multi-tree variant XMSS^MT, in enough detail to ensure interoperability between implementations. Its security does not require the hash function to be collision-resistant.
sections.eli5: Signatures built only from scrambling machines (hash functions) are small to keep and quick to check, but each signature is big.

sections.title: WOTS+: The One-Time Building Block
sections.content:
WOTS+ uses parameters n (the byte length of the message digest and of each key element) and w, the Winternitz parameter, which is 4 or 16. A larger w gives shorter signatures but slower signing. The key pair is a virtual structure of len hash chains. The private key is len random n-byte strings, each the start of a chain. The public key holds the end of each chain.

To sign, the message is turned into base-w numbers and a checksum is appended. Each number selects one node from its own chain, and the signature is those nodes together. The chaining function applies a keyed hash F repeatedly, with keys and bitmasks produced by a pseudorandom function PRF.

Each WOTS+ private key MUST be used to sign at most one message. Signing two different messages makes the scheme insecure.
sections.eli5: A WOTS+ key is like a set of ladders, and your message decides how many rungs you climb on each one. Showing where you stopped proves you know the bottom, but doing it twice lets others guess more.

sections.title: XMSS: A Tree of One-Time Keys
sections.content:
XMSS signs a fixed number of messages. Each key pair is tied to a perfect binary tree of height h, so a tree holds 2^h leaves. Each leaf holds a tree hash of a WOTS+ public key. Each inner node is made by concatenating its two children, XORing with a bitmask and applying the keyed hash H. The root, together with a public seed, forms the XMSS public key.

XMSS is stateful. The WOTS+ key pairs are numbered from 0 to 2^h - 1, and the private key holds an index of the next unused one, which is incremented with every signature. An implementation MUST NOT output the signature before the private key is updated.

An XMSS signature is 4 + n + (len + h) * n bytes: the 4-byte index, an n-byte randomizer r, the WOTS+ signature, and an authentication path of h sibling nodes. A verifier recomputes the root from the WOTS+ signature and the path, and accepts if it equals the root in the public key.
sections.eli5: The tree is a family tree of fingerprints with the key at the top. Each signature shows one stamp plus the few fingerprints needed to climb to the top and match it.

sections.title: XMSS^MT and Parameter Sets
sections.content:
XMSS^MT builds a hypertree: d layers of XMSS trees, each of height h / d. Trees on upper layers sign the roots of trees one layer below, and the lowest layer signs the actual messages. This addresses the slow key generation of a single large tree. Its signature is ceil(h / 8) + n + (h + d * len) * n bytes.

The RFC defines parameter sets for n = 32 and n = 64, always with w = 16. The REQUIRED sets use SHA2-256 and tree heights h of 10, 16 and 20. SHA2-512 and SHAKE sets are OPTIONAL. An implementation must support verification for all REQUIRED sets and MAY support signing with any proposed set. The defaults are XMSS_SHA2_20_256 and XMSSMT-SHA2_60/3_256.

A larger height allows more signatures per key pair but makes signatures bigger and key generation, signing and verification slower.
sections.eli5: For a huge number of stamps, you can build trees of trees so you only grow the small part you need first. You can pick small, medium or large books of stamps.

sections.title: Security and Post-Quantum Notes
sections.content:
Reuse of a secret key state leaves no cryptographic guarantee, and it becomes feasible to forge a signature on a new message. Developers should not use these schemes except in systems that prevent such reuse. Because the key changes over time, classical signature APIs cannot be used unchanged: the API MUST be able to return an updated secret key state.

The RFC says that any signature scheme for arbitrary-size messages relies on a hash function. For these schemes that is enough, whereas RSA, DSA and ECDSA also rely on the hardness of certain mathematical problems. For post-quantum security the size of n must be twice that needed classically, to counter square-root attacks based on Grover's algorithm. Parameters with n = 32 give post-quantum security of 128 bits and n = 64 give 256 bits.

The CFRG note states that post-quantum algorithms are considered ready for experimentation, but that there was not significant deployment experience at the time of writing.
sections.eli5: The big rule is never use a stamp twice. If the computer forgets which stamps it used, for example after restoring an old backup, anyone could copy you.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA created three registries: one for WOTS+ signatures, one for XMSS signatures and one for XMSS^MT signatures. Additions need the "Specification Required" policy from RFC 8126. Each entry has a short name, a positive number and a reference to a specification.

The number 0x00000000 is Reserved, and numbers from 0xDDDDDDDD to 0xFFFFFFFF are Reserved for Private Use. Signature and public key formats start with a 32-bit enumeration value identifying the algorithm, so the whole format can be parsed from it. A reference implementation in C is mentioned for testing.
sections.eli5: There is an official list that gives each version of the scheme a number, so two programs can agree which one they are using.
